 San Gabriel Valley foothill communities prepare for rainy weather
 By
 Laurie Perez 
 Laurie Perez 
 Laurie Perez is an award-winning journalist you'll catch most nights at 9, 10, and 11 PM reporting on CBS LA. She primarily covers the LA metro area and is a member of CBS LA's Team of journalists with a special focus on immigration issues.
 Read Full Bio 
 Laurie Perez 
 November 17, 2026 / 9:46 PM PST 
 / CBS LA
 Add CBS News on Google 
 Communities across the San Gabriel Valley foothills are preparing for this week's storm and the many others ahead.
 "You just never know with the rain," resident Glenn Brown said. "You just never really know."
 No one knows better, or in this case worse, than Brown about what can happen in Sierra Madre when a storm hits. He does not want a repeat of what happened in 2025 after the Eaton Fire. Weeks after the disaster, a stalled car clogged the road in front of his home, trapping a flood of fire debris and mud that quickly overtook his street-level office. 
 "Logs and stuff were coming down from up above," Brown said. "Burst the mud wall and my neighbor's mud wall at the same time. It was overwhelming."
 He's put his mud wall back up, while other neighbors have K-rails in place. 
 The good news this year might be that the basin above their neighborhood appears to be clear. 
 "This was all broken-down trees, branches and debris of all kinds and mud," resident Joss Rogers said. "They had to clean all of this out."
 Rogers used his drone to check out the Sierra Madre Dam area debris basin and saw that it was empty. He pointed out evidence of how full it once was. 
 "The levels got up that high, which is insane," he said. "They had like skiploaders and dump trucks and stuff coming and going on this street up here for months."
 The Los Angeles County Department of Public Works said crews removed enough sediment to fill the Rose Bowl three times.
